chapter.title: Spotting what changed

cards.body:
Acme's pricing page is 212 lines long, and overnight one price changed. Can you find it before your coffee goes cold?

Your clipper doesn't read both papers out to you. They lay yesterday's page next to today's and **cut out only what's different**. That cut is called a *diff*, and it's the scissors of your clipping service.
cards.simpler:
Acme's pricing page has 212 lines. Overnight, one price on it changed. Could you find it before your coffee goes cold?

Your clipper doesn't read both papers aloud to you. They put yesterday's page next to today's and **cut out only what's different**. That cut-out piece is called a *diff*. Think of it as the scissors of your clipping service.

cards.prompt: Your clipper has Tuesday's and Wednesday's copies of Acme's pricing page. Which note would you actually want on your desk?

options.text: All 212 lines of Wednesday's page, stapled together.
Three lines: 'Gone: Team plan $39 a month. New: Team plan $49 a month. New: Now with even more value!'

whyNot.a: That's the whole newspaper, not the clipping. You'd still have to hunt for the change yourself.
whyNot.c: That's a gut feeling, not a comparison. A $10 price rise hides easily inside 'about the same'.

cards.reteach: The clipper's job is to compare, not to copy. Put two days side by side, keep only the lines that differ and throw away the rest. The shortest note that shows what's new and what's gone wins.

cards.title: Two copies, one comparison
cards.body:
A *diff* (short for difference) is a line-by-line comparison of two text files, here yesterday's copy and today's. **It keeps only the lines that are new or gone.** Lines that match are skipped, except for a few nearby lines shown so you can see where the change sits.

Picture two sheets of tracing paper held up to a window. Where the ink lines up, you see one line. Where it doesn't, the difference jumps out.

You'd think the agent has to understand the page to spot a change. It doesn't. The diff knows nothing about prices. It only checks whether each line matches, letter for letter.
cards.simpler:
A *diff*, short for difference, compares yesterday's copy of a page with today's, line by line. **It keeps only the lines that are new or gone.** Matching lines are skipped, except a few nearby ones that show where the change sits.

Picture two sheets of tracing paper held up to a window. Where the ink doesn't line up, the difference jumps out.

The diff doesn't understand prices. It only checks whether each line matches, letter for letter.

cards.title: Acme raises a price
cards.body: Say you saved yesterday's and today's copies as acme-pricing-2026-10-03.txt and acme-pricing-2026-10-04.txt. On a Mac, Terminal (the app where you type commands) has a built-in tool for comparing them: type `diff -u` and then the two file names. The first lines start with `---` and `+++` and just name the two files, and a line starting with `@@` says where on the page the change sits, so skip those. Below them you'll find `-Team plan: $39 per user per month`, then `+Team plan: $49 per user per month`, then `+Now with even more value!`, with a few unchanged lines around them. A single minus means the line was there yesterday and is gone today, and a single plus means it's new. **Three changed lines out of 212**, and the cheerful one showed up on the same day as the $10 rise.
cards.simpler: Say you saved yesterday's and today's copies as acme-pricing-2026-10-03.txt and acme-pricing-2026-10-04.txt. On a Mac, Terminal, the app where you type commands, can compare them. Type `diff -u` and both file names. Skip the top lines starting with `---`, `+++` or `@@`. They only name the files and say where the change is. Then you'll see `-Team plan: $39 per user per month`, then `+Team plan: $49 per user per month`, then `+Now with even more value!` A single minus means gone since yesterday. A single plus means new. **Three changed lines out of 212**, and the cheerful one arrived with the $10 rise.

cards.prompt: Priya's agent has Monday's and Tuesday's copies of a rival's changelog (their list of product updates). It's about to hand something to the model to explain. What should it hand over?

options.text: Tuesday's full copy, so nothing gets missed.
Only the changed lines from the diff, the ones starting with a single + or -.
Monday's full copy, since it's already been checked.

whyNot.a: That's the newspaper, not the clipping. The change is in there, but it's buried under everything that stayed the same.
whyNot.c: That's yesterday's paper. Nothing new can be in it, because the news only arrived on Tuesday.

cards.reteach: Only what moved should travel on. Compare Monday with Tuesday, keep the + lines (new) and the - lines (gone), and drop everything else, including the file-name lines at the top. The model gets a clipping, not a pile of newspapers.

cards.title: Lines that change for no reason
cards.body:
A diff is honest but very literal. If the page says *Updated 4 October* at the top, that line changes every day, so the diff will flag it every day.

Your clipper knows the date on a newspaper's front page isn't news. Your agent doesn't know that until you tell it. Before comparing, **remove the lines you know change by themselves**: dates, view counters, a customer quote that rotates.

The opposite trap is a redesign. When a rival rebuilds their site, nearly every line changes at once. That isn't 200 pieces of news. It's one: the page got rebuilt.
cards.simpler:
A diff is honest but literal. If the page says *Updated 4 October* at the top, that line changes daily, so the diff flags it daily.

Your clipper knows the date on a front page isn't news. Your agent needs telling. Before comparing, **remove the lines you know change by themselves**: dates, view counters, a rotating customer quote.

Beware the opposite trap. When a rival rebuilds their site, nearly every line changes. That's one piece of news, not 200.

cards.body: Sam's agent compares each new copy with the very first one saved on day 1, not with yesterday's. Acme raises a price on Tuesday, and the same 'price went up' note lands on Sam's desk on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. **If one change shows up two days in a row, check which file is being used as the 'old' one.** It should always be yesterday's copy.
cards.simpler: Sam's agent compares each new copy with the very first one, saved on day 1, instead of yesterday's. Acme raises a price on Tuesday. Then the same 'price went up' note lands on Sam's desk on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. It's like checking today's paper against last month's and calling old news new. **If one change shows up two days running, check which file is being used as the 'old' one.** It should always be yesterday's copy.

cards.prompt: This morning's diff of a rival's pricing page has just one changed line: `-Free trial: 14 days`. What happened?

options.text: The free trial line was there yesterday and is gone today.
Nothing. That line is the same as yesterday.

whyNot.a: That would be a plus line, not a minus. + means new, - means gone.
whyNot.c: That would be a matching line, not a changed one. Lines that didn't change don't get a + or a -.

cards.reteach: Read the first character like a tag on a clipping. A minus is a line from yesterday that has disappeared. A plus is a line from today that wasn't there before. So '-Free trial' means the trial line has gone, which could be the biggest news of the week.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Every morning the agent lays yesterday's saved copy next to today's and keeps only the lines marked + (new) or - (gone). Remove the lines that change by themselves, like dates, and **the scissors cut out only real news**.
cards.simpler: Every morning, the agent puts yesterday's saved copy next to today's. It keeps only the lines marked + (new) or - (gone). Take out the lines that change on their own, like dates, and **the scissors cut out only real news**.

cards.body:
Open Terminal on your Mac. Make two short text files, a.txt and b.txt, that match except for one line. Type `diff -u a.txt b.txt` and **find your change** among the lines starting with a single + or -. Skip the --- and +++ lines at the top; they just name the files.

Tomorrow: why a price rise and a fixed typo look exactly the same in a diff.
cards.simpler:
Open Terminal on your Mac. Make two short text files, a.txt and b.txt, that are the same except for one line. Type `diff -u a.txt b.txt` and press Return. Skip the top lines starting with --- and +++, which just name the files. Then look through the lines starting with a single + or - and **find your change**. The minus line is the old version, and the plus line is the new one.

dubious_claims: Card 1 says one line changed, but card 4 shows three changed lines (- $39, + $49, + 'Now with even more value!').
Card 2's 'right' answer shows two lines for the same Acme Team plan change, but card 4 shows three for it.
Real `diff -u` output puts no space after the + or - (e.g. `-Team plan: $39...`). The chapter's `- Team plan` would mean the original line started with a space.

Real `diff -u` output also prints header lines starting with --- and +++ and position lines starting with @@. These would confuse a reader told that every - or + line is a change, and they get no warning.
Card 7 says the diff has 'just one line', but real `diff -u` output always adds headers and up to 3 unchanged lines around the change, so it can't be one line.
Card 4's 'In chapter 3 you saved acme-pricing-2026-10-03.txt...' points to a chapter not shown here, so I couldn't check it.
Open loop: the 'Tomorrow:' teaser sits in card 8, not at the end. The chapter actually ends on the try card and the outcome line.
repairedFrom.why: The hook says 'overnight one line changed', but card 4 shows three changed lines out of 212 (one gone, two new). The chapter's opening promise and its own worked example disagree.
repairedFrom.fix: Change 'overnight one line changed' to 'overnight one price changed', so the hook stays sharp and matches the three-line diff in card 4.
